notes.text: I'm a computer engineer. I took a chip-design class. Of course I know everything about chip design. I do not know anything about chip design. All I know is a chip package is a few small chips, chiplets, that get hot, and you can't put them too close together or too far apart. But I'll tell you what: my agents know chip design.
notes.cue: Pause after "everything about chip design." Then, deadpan: "I do not know anything about chip design." Let the last line land. Before the talk: one real timed rehearsal with the actual demo.

content.title: What agents need, and only what they are allowed to touch.
content.footer: What Senti does for every agent in the room.
chips: Drift and rogue agents handled gracefully

notes.text: I'm building Senti. It recognizes agents, sets them up, lets them collaborate, serves what they need, and keeps a record of what they did. Delegation is scoped; drift and rogue agents are handled gracefully, because each only gets what it's allowed to touch. Shopping, security, and today, science.

notes.text: They localized a difference around the modeled link between the metal lid and cooler. Then they started discussing spreader-to-sink coupling. Which sounds like a plumbing emergency, but apparently it can ruin your experiment. Two other teams reported results from changing that link.

content.title: Passing one check isn't passing them all.
content.footer: Delfie (delphisci team) reports the one-step change; ScienceClaw reports reproducing it and computed its heat balance. The figure carries each column's own reading and limits.
content.label: simulated, not silicon

figure.alt: Three versions against three checks on the CPU-DRAM design. Older version, our pinned 6.0 build: 0.01 degrees off the paper, passing the 1 degree bar set in advance; heat out exceeds heat in by 1.39 percent, failing the balance check; 6.3 degrees from three separate solvers. Newer version 7.0: 117 degrees off the paper, failing; heat balances within rounding; 102 degrees from the solvers. Newer version with one step changed, as Delfie reports and ScienceClaw reports too: 9.6 degrees off the paper, failing; heat balances within rounding, as ScienceClaw reports; 3.3 degrees from the solvers. Saved 45 mm, grid 64 CPU-DRAM cases, simulated, not compared with a real chip. The heat check's rounding limit is about 0.43 watts, 0.063 percent, and is not a total error bound. Each column uses its own reading. The paper column uses the native all-block reading, 232.67 degrees for 7.0. The solver column uses the hottest chiplet entry, 224.67 degrees for 7.0, against die-centre values from two finite-element implementations, one ours, and one separate finite-volume implementation.

notes.text: Our fixed reference test with the older setup reproduced two published values within a hundredth of a degree. Our saved older-build result matched the paper but failed this heat-balance check. The modified output is reported within rounding and nearer the separate solvers; it still misses the paper. Source analysis found non-reciprocal lateral links consistent with that. I nodded.

content.title: Other solvers: descriptive, not a verdict.
items: Two finite-element implementations and a separate finite-volume implementation report about 78 and 122 degrees for these two designs. Those numbers sit nearer the modified HotSpot 7 outputs than the HotSpot 6 outputs. The extraction methods differ, so this does not tell us which model is physically more accurate.
What is compared: die-centre readings from those implementations against HotSpot's selector values.
Whose: one finite-element implementation is ours; the other is an outside team's, and the finite-volume implementation is another outside team's, unnamed until it consents.
Differences, descriptive only: about 0.7 and 3.3 degrees from the modified 7.0, and about 2.6 and 6.3 degrees from 6.0.
